title: Theorem A
body_md: Let $ABC$ be a non-equilateral spherical triangle with sides shorter than $2\beta$. The triangle $XYZ$ of the outward construction is equilateral if and only if $\cos(\Theta+\Omega/2)=0$; for the inward construction the condition is $\cos(\Theta-\Omega/2)=0$. In this case $XYZ$ is nondegenerate, and its side $\ell$ satisfies $\cos\ell=\sigma\cos\beta/(1-\sigma\cos\beta)$, where $\sigma=\pm1$ is the sine of $\Theta\pm\Omega/2$.
head: environment

title: Theorem B
body_md:
Let $ABC$ be as in Theorem~A, and let $\varepsilon=1$ for the outward and $\varepsilon=-1$ for the inward construction.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item The construction with sign $\varepsilon$ gives an equilateral $XYZ$ if and only if, for some $\kappa\in\{\cos\beta,-\cos\beta\}$, we have $(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_\kappa$ and $\varepsilon\kappa(x+y+z-xyz)>0$. Conversely, every point of $\mathcal{Q}_\kappa$ in $(0,\tan\beta)^3$, outside the diagonal $x=y=z$ and the surface $x+y+z=xyz$, determines a spherical triangle whose construction with sign $\varepsilon=\operatorname{sign}(\kappa(x+y+z-xyz))$ gives an equilateral $XYZ$.
\item If $\beta\le\pi/3$, non-equilateral solutions only occur in the outward construction. They form a two-parameter family, parametrized by the part of the ellipsoid $\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}$ in the open positive octant with its diagonal point removed. For $\beta=\pi/3$ this is the family of \cite{DNV24}.
\item If $\beta>\pi/3$, there are two outward families and one inward family, and a second inward family exists if and only if $\cos\beta<1/4$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem:area
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:poly
title: Proof
body_md:
For all real $p,q,r$ we have the polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:poly}
2(1+p)(1+q)(1+r)-(1+p+q+r)^2=1+2pqr-p^2-q^2-r^2 .
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{eq:gram} and $2\cos^2(a/2)=1+p$, it gives $\alpha^2+\delta^2=16g^2$. On the other hand, the solid-angle formula of van Oosterom and Strackee \cite{vOS83} reads
\[
\frac{\Omega}{2}=\operatorname{Arg}(\alpha+i\delta)\in(0,\pi),
\]
the argument lying in $(0,\pi)$ since $\delta>0$. For $\alpha\ne0$ this is the relation $\tan(\Omega/2)=\delta/\alpha$, and for $\alpha=0$ it gives $\Omega=\pi$; the latter case does occur, e.g.~for $p=q=-3/5$ and $r=1/5$. Combining the argument and the modulus, we obtain \eqref{eq:area}. Note that its real and imaginary parts, $\cos(\Omega/2)=\alpha/(4g)$ and $\sin(\Omega/2)=\delta/(4g)$, are the classical half-area formulas of Euler and Cagnoli \cite{Tod86}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $B,C\in\mathbb{S}^2$ be distinct and not antipodal. A point $D\in\mathbb{S}^2$ is a \emph{$\beta$-point} of $BC$ if $|DB|=|DC|$ and the Euclidean angle $\angle BDC$ equals $\beta$.
head: environment

label: lem:construction
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first define a candidate $X$ by the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:X}, and then show that it is the circumcentre of the chosen $D,B,C$. The vectors $B+C$ and $B\times C$ are orthogonal, with squared lengths $2(1+p)$ and $1-p^2$, so that \eqref{eq:x} gives
\[
|x(B+C)-\varepsilon B\times C|^2=(1+p)(2x^2+1-p)=4\sin^2\beta\cos^2\beta\,(1+x^2)^2=\bigl(\tan\beta\,(1+p)\bigr)^2 .
\]
Thus $|X|=1$, and $\langle X,B\rangle=\langle X,C\rangle=x\cot\beta=\mathrel{\mathop:} t\in(0,1)$. Let $\Gamma=\{\langle X,U\rangle=t\}\cap\mathbb{S}^2$, with centre $G=tX$ and radius $R=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Using \eqref{eq:x}, we get
\[
\cos\angle BGC=\frac{\langle B-G,C-G\rangle}{R^2}=\frac{p-t^2}{1-t^2}=\cos2\beta,
\]
so that the spherical angle $BXC$ equals $2\beta$.

The component of $X$ in the plane spanned by $B,C$ is a positive multiple of $B+C$. Hence the perpendicular from $X$ to the great circle $BC$ meets the shorter arc at its midpoint $(B+C)/|B+C|$, and divides $XBC$ into two right triangles, each with hypotenuse $d(X,B)$, angle $\beta$ at $X$, and leg $a/2$ opposite to $X$. If $\theta_a$ denotes the angle at $B$, the second rule in \eqref{eq:napier} gives $\cot\beta\cot\theta_a=\cos d(X,B)=x\cot\beta$. Hence $\cot\theta_a=x>0$, and $\theta_a$ is acute. The first rule gives $\cos\beta=\cos(a/2)\sin\theta_a$.

Let $M=(B+C)/2$. Since the central angle is $2\beta<\pi$, we have $|G-M|=R\cos\beta$, so that the point $D'=G+\sec\beta\,(G-M)$ lies on $\Gamma$. It lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, beyond $G$ as seen from $M$, hence on the major arc determined by the chord $BC$. The inscribed angle theorem gives $\angle BD'C=\beta$, and $|D'B|=|D'C|$ by symmetry. Finally, $\langle X,B\times C\rangle=-\varepsilon(1-p)/\tan\beta$ and $\langle D',B\times C\rangle=(1+\sec\beta)\,t\,\langle X,B\times C\rangle$ both have the sign of $-\varepsilon$. We conclude that $D'$ is the chosen $\beta$-point $D$, and that $X$ is its spherical circumcentre. Expanding the expression for $D'$ gives (iii).

title: Remark

title: Theorem

label: rem:branches
title: Remark
head: environment

label: thm:quadric
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:quadric}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item Let $ABC$ be a non-equilateral spherical triangle satisfying \eqref{eq:domain}. The construction with sign $\varepsilon$ gives an equilateral triangle $XYZ$ if and only if, for some $\kappa\in\{\cos\beta,-\cos\beta\}$,
\[
(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_\kappa \text{ and } \varepsilon\kappa(x+y+z-xyz)>0 .
\]
In this case $\kappa=-\sigma\cos\beta$ and $\cos\ell=-\kappa/(1+\kappa)$.
\item Conversely, let $(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_\kappa$ with $0<x,y,z<\tan\beta$, not all equal, and $x+y+z\ne xyz$. Then there is a spherical triangle, unique up to isometry, with side cosines $2\cos^2\beta\,(1+x^2)-1$, $2\cos^2\beta\,(1+y^2)-1$, $2\cos^2\beta\,(1+z^2)-1$. It satisfies \eqref{eq:domain}, and its construction with $\varepsilon=\operatorname{sign}(\kappa(x+y+z-xyz))$ gives an equilateral $XYZ$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: cor:small
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:small}
Let $0<\beta\le\pi/3$, and let $ABC$ be non-equilateral and satisfy \eqref{eq:domain}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The inward construction never gives an equilateral $XYZ$.
\item The outward construction gives one if and only if $\Theta+\Omega/2=3\pi/2$, i.e.~if and only if $(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}$. In this case $\cos\ell=-\cos\beta/(1+\cos\beta)$.
\item The quadric $\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}$ is an ellipsoid, and each of its points in the open positive octant, except the diagonal one, comes from a triangle as in (ii). In particular, these triangles form a two-parameter family.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: cor:large
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:large}
Let $\pi/3<\beta<\pi/2$. Within the cube $(0,\tan\beta)^3$, consider the four sets
\[
\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}\cap\{e_1>e_3\},\ \mathcal{Q}_{-\cos\beta}\cap\{e_1<e_3\},\ \mathcal{Q}_{-\cos\beta}\cap\{e_1>e_3\},\ \mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}\cap\{e_1<e_3\},
\]
which correspond to the outward, outward, inward and inward construction respectively. The first three contain a two-dimensional set of non-diagonal points, and the last one contains non-diagonal points if and only if $\cos\beta<1/4$. In particular, the outward construction gives equilateral triangles of two different sizes, and so does the inward one when $\cos\beta<1/4$.
head: environment

label: rem:both
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:both}
A non-equilateral $ABC$ gives equilateral triangles of centres in both constructions if and only if $\Theta=\Omega=\pi$. Indeed, by \eqref{eq:branches}, the outward and inward values of $\Phi$ lie in $\{\pi/2,3\pi/2\}$ and $\{-\pi/2,\pi/2\}$ respectively. Their difference is $\Omega\in(0,2\pi)$ and their sum is $2\Theta>0$, so that they must be $3\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$; the converse follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:angle}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:area} and \eqref{eq:product}, this condition is equivalent to $\alpha=0$ and $e_2=1$. To express it on the quadrics, put $c_\beta=\cos\beta$. The algebraic identity \eqref{eq:alphaQ}, proved independently below, gives
\[
2Q_{c_\beta}=\alpha-4c_\beta^3(1-e_2),\ \ 2Q_{-c_\beta}=\alpha+4c_\beta^3(1-e_2),
\]
so that the condition is also equivalent to $(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}\cap\mathcal{Q}_{-\cos\beta}$. Since the inward value of $\Phi$ gives $\sigma=1$, this forces $\beta>\pi/3$. Example~\ref{ex:both} provides an explicit instance.

label: lem:inner
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We take the inner product of the numerator in \eqref{eq:X} with its cyclic counterpart. The four terms are given by $\langle B+C,C+A\rangle=\alpha$, $\langle B+C,C\times A\rangle=\langle B\times C,C+A\rangle=\delta$ and $\langle B\times C,C\times A\rangle=pq-r$, which gives the first expression in \eqref{eq:XY}; the second one follows from \eqref{eq:x}.
head: environment

label: lem:difference
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:difference}
Let $J=\alpha(e_1-e_3)-\varepsilon\delta(1-e_2)$. Then
\[
(1+z^2)N_{xy}-(1+y^2)N_{zx}=(y-z)J,
\]
and the same holds after cyclically permuting $x,y,z$ together with $a,b,c$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We compare the terms of $N_{xy}$ and $N_{zx}$. The terms involving $\alpha$ give $xy(1+z^2)-xz(1+y^2)=x(y-z)(1-yz)$, and those involving $\delta$ give $(x+y)(1+z^2)-(x+z)(1+y^2)=(y-z)(1-e_2)$. For the remaining terms, recall from \eqref{eq:x} that $1+z^2=(1+r)/(2\cos^2\beta)$ and $1+y^2=(1+q)/(2\cos^2\beta)$, and note the identity
\[
(1+r)(pq-r)-(1+q)(rp-q)=(q-r)\alpha .
\]
Since $q-r=2\cos^2\beta\,(y^2-z^2)$, these terms contribute $\alpha(y-z)(y+z)$. The total is $(y-z)[\alpha(x(1-yz)+y+z)-\varepsilon\delta(1-e_2)]=(y-z)J$.
head: environment

label: lem:J
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:J}
Let $S=\sin\theta_a\sin\theta_b\sin\theta_c$ and $\Phi=\Theta+\varepsilon\Omega/2$. Then
\[
(\alpha-i\varepsilon\delta)\bigl((1-e_2)+i(e_1-e_3)\bigr)=-\frac{4g}{S}(\sin\Phi+i\cos\Phi).
\]
In particular, $J=-(4g/S)\cos\Phi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:area} we have $\alpha-i\varepsilon\delta=4g\,e^{-i\varepsilon\Omega/2}$, and by \eqref{eq:product} we have $(1-e_2)+i(e_1-e_3)=-i\,e^{-i\Theta}/S$. Their product is $-i(4g/S)e^{-i\Phi}$, whose imaginary part is $J$.
head: environment

label: lem:identities
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:x}, we have $\alpha=2\kappa^2(3+x^2+y^2+z^2)-2$, and \eqref{eq:alphaQ} reduces to $-2+6\kappa^2-4\kappa^3=-2(1-\kappa)^2(1+2\kappa)$.

For \eqref{eq:NQ}, we substitute $\alpha=4\kappa^3(1-e_2)+2Q_\kappa$ and $\varepsilon\delta=4\kappa^3(e_1-e_3)$. Since $(1-e_2)xy-(e_1-e_3)(x+y)=xy-x^2y^2-(x+y)^2-z(x+y)$, we get
\[
N_{xy}=2xyQ_\kappa+4\kappa^3\bigl(xy-x^2y^2-(x+y)^2\bigr)-4\kappa^3z(x+y)+pq-r .
\]
The variable $z$ also occurs in $-r=1-2\kappa^2(1+z^2)$, and
\[
-4\kappa^3z(x+y)-2\kappa^2z^2=-2Q_\kappa-2(1-\kappa)^2(1+2\kappa)+2\kappa^2(x^2+y^2)+4\kappa^3xy .
\]
After this substitution, $N_{xy}-2(xy-1)Q_\kappa$ no longer involves $z$, and equals
\[
4\kappa^3\bigl(2xy-x^2y^2-(x+y)^2\bigr)+pq+1-2\kappa^2-2(1-\kappa)^2(1+2\kappa)+2\kappa^2(x^2+y^2).
\]
Substituting $p=2\kappa^2(1+x^2)-1$ and $q=2\kappa^2(1+y^2)-1$, this expression reduces to $-4\kappa^3(1-\kappa)(1+x^2)(1+y^2)$, which proves \eqref{eq:NQ}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:inner} and~\ref{lem:difference}, the equality $\langle X,Y\rangle=\langle X,Z\rangle$ is equivalent to $(y-z)J=0$, and the other two equalities are equivalent to $(z-x)J=0$ and $(x-y)J=0$. Since $ABC$ is not equilateral, the coordinates $x,y,z$ are not all equal. We deduce that the three pairwise distances are equal if and only if $J=0$, i.e.~by Lemma~\ref{lem:J}, if and only if $\cos\Phi=0$.

We now assume that $\cos\Phi=0$, and let $\sigma=\sin\Phi$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:J}, the product $(\alpha-i\varepsilon\delta)((1-e_2)+i(e_1-e_3))=-4\sigma g/S$ is real. Since the second factor has squared modulus $(1+x^2)(1+y^2)(1+z^2)=S^{-2}$, we get
\[
\alpha-i\varepsilon\delta=-4\sigma gS\bigl((1-e_2)-i(e_1-e_3)\bigr).
\]
By \eqref{eq:theta}, we have $gS=\cos^3\beta$. Letting $\kappa=-\sigma\cos\beta$, this reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alpha-delta}
\alpha=4\kappa^3(1-e_2), \ \ \varepsilon\delta=4\kappa^3(e_1-e_3).
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:alphaQ}, we have $Q_\kappa=0$, and \eqref{eq:NQ} and \eqref{eq:XY} then give
\[
\langle X,Y\rangle=\frac{-4\kappa^3(1-\kappa)}{4\kappa^2(1-\kappa^2)}=-\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}=\mathrel{\mathop:}\rho ,
\]
and the same value for the other two pairs. This is \eqref{eq:side}.

It remains to show that $XYZ$ is nondegenerate. If $\sigma=1$, then $\rho=\cos\beta/(1-\cos\beta)\le1$ forces $\cos\beta\le1/2$. Equality would give $X=Y=Z$; since $\langle X,C\rangle=x\cot\beta$ and $\langle Y,C\rangle=y\cot\beta$, this would force $x=y$, and similarly $y=z$, which is impossible. Hence $\beta>\pi/3$ and $0<\rho<1$. If $\sigma=-1$, then $-1/2<\rho<0$. In both cases the Gram matrix of $X,Y,Z$, whose eigenvalues are $1-\rho,1-\rho,1+2\rho$, is positive definite, and we conclude that $XYZ$ is nondegenerate.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) If $XYZ$ is equilateral, the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:angle} gives $Q_\kappa=0$ and $\varepsilon\delta=4\kappa^3(e_1-e_3)$ with $\kappa=-\sigma\cos\beta$. Since $\delta>0$, the numbers $\varepsilon$ and $\kappa(e_1-e_3)$ have the same sign.

Conversely, assume that $Q_\kappa=0$ and $\varepsilon\kappa(e_1-e_3)>0$. By \eqref{eq:alphaQ}, we have $\alpha=4\kappa^3(1-e_2)$. On the other hand, Lemma~\ref{lem:area}, \eqref{eq:x} and \eqref{eq:product} give
\[
\alpha^2+\delta^2=2(1+p)(1+q)(1+r)=16\kappa^6(1+x^2)(1+y^2)(1+z^2)=16\kappa^6\bigl((1-e_2)^2+(e_1-e_3)^2\bigr).
\]
Hence $\delta=4|\kappa^3(e_1-e_3)|$, and the sign condition gives $\varepsilon\delta=4\kappa^3(e_1-e_3)$. It follows that $J=0$, and $XYZ$ is equilateral by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:angle}.

(b) We define $p,q,r$ by the stated formulas. The bounds $1<1+x^2<\sec^2\beta$ give $-1<p<1$, and similarly for $q,r$. To establish the existence of a triangle, we combine \eqref{eq:poly} and \eqref{eq:alphaQ} with the algebraic identity $(1+x^2)(1+y^2)(1+z^2)=(1-e_2)^2+(e_1-e_3)^2$ from \eqref{eq:product}. This gives
\[
1+2pqr-p^2-q^2-r^2=2(1+p)(1+q)(1+r)-\alpha^2=16\kappa^6(e_1-e_3)^2>0 .
\]
The Gram criterion of \S\ref{sec:prelim} now provides a triangle with these side cosines, unique up to isometry. The positivity of $x,y,z$ gives \eqref{eq:domain}, and the coordinates computed from its sides are the original $x,y,z$. Since they are not all equal, the triangle is not equilateral, and we conclude by applying (a) with $\varepsilon=\operatorname{sign}(\kappa(e_1-e_3))$.

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof we write $c=\cos\beta\in(0,1/2)$. For $\kappa=\pm c$, the two eigenvalues and $K_\kappa$ are positive, so that both quadrics are ellipsoids. The strict inequalities defining the four parts give relatively open subsets of these surfaces. We show that the first three parts are nonempty in the admissible cube, and determine when the fourth one is.

$\mathcal{Q}_c\cap\{e_1>e_3\}$: by \eqref{eq:K-bound} we have $0<\sqrt{K_c}<\tan\beta$. For small $x,y>0$ with $x\ne y$, the point $(x,y,z(x,y))$ given by \eqref{eq:zxy} with $\kappa=c$ lies on $\mathcal{Q}_c$ and in the open cube, and $e_1-e_3$ is close to $\sqrt{K_c}>0$.

$\mathcal{Q}_{-c}\cap\{e_1>e_3\}$: here $K_{-c}=(1+c)^2(1-2c)/c^2>0$, and $K_{-c}<\tan^2\beta$ is equivalent to $(1+c)(1-2c)<1-c$, i.e.~to $2c^2>0$. We then use \eqref{eq:zxy} with $\kappa=-c$ near $(0,0,\sqrt{K_{-c}})$ as before.

$\mathcal{Q}_{-c}\cap\{e_1<e_3\}$: the positive diagonal point of $\mathcal{Q}_{-c}$ is $(t,t,t)$, where $t=(1+c)/(\sqrt3\,c)$. Since $c<1/2$, we have $t>\sqrt3$ and $e_1-e_3=t(3-t^2)<0$. Moreover $t<\tan\beta$, because $(1+c)^2<3(1-c^2)$. A sufficiently small neighbourhood of this point on the ellipsoid remains in the open cube and satisfies $e_1<e_3$, and removing the diagonal point leaves a two-dimensional set of admissible points.

$\mathcal{Q}_c\cap\{e_1<e_3\}$: if $c\ge1/4$, then \eqref{eq:e2-bound} gives $e_2\le(1-c)^2/c^2\le9$, and the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality $e_1e_2\ge9e_3$, with equality only for $x=y=z$, gives $e_3\le e_1e_2/9\le e_1$; hence there are no non-diagonal points. If $c<1/4$, the diagonal point $t=(1-c)/(\sqrt3\,c)>\sqrt3$ of $\mathcal{Q}_c$ satisfies $e_1<e_3$ and lies in the open cube by \eqref{eq:K-bound}, and the argument of the previous case applies.

The statement about the two sizes follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:quadric}(a).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inequality $\cos\ell<0$ forces $\sigma=-1$ in \eqref{eq:side}. We may therefore take $\kappa=\cos\beta$ in \eqref{eq:alpha-delta}, and $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\kappa/(1+\kappa)$. Formula~\eqref{eq:X} gives $\langle X,C+A\rangle=(x\alpha-\varepsilon\delta)/(\tan\beta\,(1+p))$. Using \eqref{eq:alpha-delta} and the identity $x(1-e_2)-(e_1-e_3)=-(1+x^2)(y+z)$, we obtain $x\alpha-\varepsilon\delta=-4\kappa^3(1+x^2)(y+z)$, and hence
\[
\langle X,C+A\rangle=-2\kappa(y+z)\cot\beta, \text{ and similarly } \langle Y,B+C\rangle=-2\kappa(x+z)\cot\beta .
\]
Using Lemma~\ref{lem:construction}(iii), $\sec\beta=1/\kappa$ and $\cot^2\beta=\kappa^2/(1-\kappa^2)$, we get
\begin{align*}
\langle D,E\rangle&=\frac{(1+\kappa)^2}{\kappa^2}xy\cot^2\beta\,\langle X,Y\rangle-\frac{1+\kappa}{2\kappa^2}\cot\beta\bigl(x\langle X,C+A\rangle+y\langle Y,B+C\rangle\bigr)+\frac{\alpha}{4\kappa^2}\\
&=\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}\bigl(-xy+x(y+z)+y(x+z)\bigr)+\kappa(1-e_2)=\kappa+\frac{\kappa^2e_2}{1-\kappa}.
\end{align*}
This expression is symmetric in $x,y,z$, so that the three pairwise inner products of $D,E,F$ are equal, with the value given in \eqref{eq:DEF}. Since $e_2>0$, their common value $\rho_D$ is greater than $\cos\beta$. Since $ABC$ is not equilateral, the inequality \eqref{eq:e2-bound} is strict, and it gives $\rho_D<1$. Thus $\cos\beta<\rho_D<1$, and the Gram eigenvalues $1-\rho_D,1-\rho_D,1+2\rho_D$ are positive. We conclude that $DEF$ is nondegenerate, and that its side satisfies $0<m<\beta$.

label: ex:DNV
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:DNV}
Take $(x,y,z)=\frac{\sqrt2}{5}(1,2,3)$ on the ellipsoid $x^2+y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx=2$. Then $e_2=22/25$, and the side cosines are $-23/50$, $-17/50$, $-7/50$, so that the sides are approximately $117.39^\circ$, $109.88^\circ$, $98.05^\circ$. This is the triangle of \cite[Example~1.6]{DNV24}. Its base angles are approximately $74.21^\circ$, $60.50^\circ$, $49.68^\circ$, so that $\Theta\approx184.40^\circ$, and $\Omega\approx171.21^\circ$; the exact relation is $\Theta+\Omega/2=270^\circ$. The outward centres have common inner product $-1/3$, and $\cos m=(1+e_2)/2=47/50$. We refer to Figure~\ref{fig:dnv} for a picture.
head: environment

label: ex:both
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:both}
Let $\cos^2\beta=11/60$, so that $\beta\approx64.65^\circ$, and take $\cos a=\cos b=-3/5$ and $\cos c=1/5$. The sides of $ABC$ are approximately $126.87^\circ$, $126.87^\circ$, $78.46^\circ$. We have $(x,y,z)=(1,1,5)/\sqrt{11}$, $e_2=1$, $e_1-e_3=72/(11\sqrt{11})>0$ and $\alpha=0$. Hence $\Theta=\Omega=180^\circ$, and the parameter point lies on both quadrics. The outward triangle of centres has $\cos\ell=-\cos\beta/(1+\cos\beta)$, i.e.~$\ell\approx107.45^\circ$, while the inward one has $\cos\ell=\cos\beta/(1-\cos\beta)$, i.e.~$\ell\approx41.51^\circ$. The sign condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:quadric} selects $\mathcal{Q}_{\cos\beta}$ for the outward construction and $\mathcal{Q}_{-\cos\beta}$ for the inward one. Accordingly, the outward $DEF$ is equilateral, with $\cos m=\cos\beta/(1-\cos\beta)$, whereas the inward $DEF$ is not: its pairwise inner products are approximately $-0.6468$, $-0.2391$, $-0.2391$.
head: environment
name: both constructions

label: ex:second
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:second}
The point $(2,\frac83,\frac{10}9)$ lies on $\mathcal{Q}_{-1/3}$, and $e_1-e_3=-4/27<0$. Its side cosines are $1/9$, $65/81$, $-367/729$, so that the sides are approximately $83.62^\circ$, $36.63^\circ$, $120.23^\circ$. Here $\Theta\approx89.11^\circ$ and $\Omega\approx1.78^\circ$, and the exact relation is $\Theta+\Omega/2=90^\circ$. Thus the outward $XYZ$ is equilateral with side $60^\circ$. The triangle $DEF$ has sides approximately $54.53^\circ$, $127.22^\circ$, $167.24^\circ$, so it is not equilateral. For comparison, the point $(1,2,\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{3})\in\mathcal{Q}_{1/3}$ satisfies $e_1-e_3>0$ and gives an outward equilateral $XYZ$ with $\cos\ell=-1/4$. These two inputs realize the two outward sizes for the same $\beta$.
head: environment
name: $\cos\beta=1/3$, second outward family

label: ex:fourth
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:fourth}
We now take $\cos\beta=1/5<1/4$. The point $(\frac43,2,\frac{10}3)$ lies on $\mathcal{Q}_{1/5}$, whose equation is $5(x^2+y^2+z^2)+2e_2=112$, and $e_1-e_3=-20/9<0$. The side cosines are $-7/9$, $-3/5$, $-7/225$, so that the sides are approximately $141.06^\circ$, $126.87^\circ$, $91.78^\circ$. The area is $\Omega\approx340.27^\circ$, while the base angles $\operatorname{arccot}(4/3)$, $\operatorname{arccot}2$, $\operatorname{arccot}(10/3)$ have sum $\Theta\approx80.13^\circ$. Thus $\Theta-\Omega/2=-90^\circ$, and the inward $XYZ$ is equilateral with $\cos\ell=-1/6$. Proposition~\ref{prop:DEF} shows that $DEF$ is equilateral as well, with $\cos m=8/9$.

name: $\cos\beta=1/5$, second inward family

label: rem:limit
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:limit}
We keep $\beta$ fixed and consider triangles with $a=\rho a_0+o(\rho)$, $b=\rho b_0+o(\rho)$, $c=\rho c_0+o(\rho)$ as $\rho\to0$, where $a_0,b_0,c_0$ are the sides of a nondegenerate Euclidean triangle. We put $\operatorname{diam}=\max(a,b,c)$. Then $\Omega\to0$ and each base angle tends to $\pi/2-\beta$. For either construction, $\cos\Phi\to\cos(3\pi/2-3\beta)=-\sin3\beta$, which is nonzero unless $\beta=\pi/3$. For $\beta=\pi/3$, the next term explains the relation with the planar theorem. From $\sin\theta_a=1/(2\cos(a/2))$ we obtain $\theta_a=\pi/6+a^2/(8\sqrt3)+O(a^4)$. Let $\Delta$ be the area of the Euclidean triangle with sides $a,b,c$, and put $s_0=(a+b+c)/2$. L'Huilier's formula
\[
\tan\frac\Omega4=\sqrt{\tan\frac{s_0}{2}\tan\frac{s_0-a}{2}\tan\frac{s_0-b}{2}\tan\frac{s_0-c}{2}}
\]
and Heron's formula give $\Omega=\Delta+O(\operatorname{diam}^4)$. Therefore, for the inward construction,
\[
\Theta-\frac\Omega2-\frac\pi2=\frac{1}{8\sqrt3}\bigl(a^2+b^2+c^2-4\sqrt3\,\Delta\bigr)+O(\operatorname{diam}^4).
\]
The quadratic term is nonnegative by Weitzenb\"ock's inequality \cite{BDJ+69}, and vanishes if and only if $a=b=c$. In other words, to leading order it measures how far the inward construction is from the equation $\Theta-\Omega/2=\pi/2$. For the outward construction, $\Theta+\Omega/2$ tends to $\pi/2$, whereas its only admissible value is $3\pi/2$. We stress that the expansion only describes this limiting behaviour; the exact exclusion of non-equilateral inward solutions is Corollary~\ref{cor:small}.

body_md: The appendix proves the angle criterion by composing the rotations about $X,Y,Z$, and uses quaternions to compute the composition. Can this argument be replaced by a synthetic proof?

title: Question
body_md: What is the corresponding classification in the hyperbolic plane? The Euclidean chord-angle definition of a $\beta$-point has no direct intrinsic analogue, but Remark~\ref{rem:equivalent} suggests erecting isosceles hyperbolic triangles with apex angle $2\beta$. Their base angles are automatically smaller than $\pi/2-\beta$, so that there is no ambiguity between acute and obtuse base angles. For $\beta=\pi/3$, this construction should be compared with \cite{DNV25}.

body_md: For which $ABC$ and $\beta$ is $DEF$ equilateral? Proposition~\ref{prop:DEF} gives a sufficient condition, but Remark~\ref{rem:DEF}(2) shows that the answer extends beyond inputs with equilateral $XYZ$.

label: lem:factor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:factor}
We have $q_X=h_{BC}\,r_B\bigl(-\varepsilon(\pi/2-\theta_a)\bigr)$, and cyclically.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $h_{BC}=(\cos(a/2),\sin(a/2)\,n)$, where $n=(B\times C)/\sin a$, and put $\mu=-\varepsilon(\pi/2-\theta_a)$, so that $\cos\mu=\sin\theta_a$ and $\sin\mu=-\varepsilon\cos\theta_a$. As $n\perp B$, the real part of $h_{BC}r_B(\mu)$ is $\cos(a/2)\sin\theta_a=\cos\beta$. For its vector part, we use $n\times B=(C-pB)/\sin a$ and $2\cos^2(a/2)=1+p$ to obtain
\[
\cos\tfrac a2\sin\mu\,B+\cos\mu\sin\tfrac a2\,n+\sin\tfrac a2\sin\mu\,n\times B
=\frac{-\varepsilon\cos\theta_a\,(B+C)+\sin\theta_a\,B\times C}{2\cos\frac a2}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:theta}, we have $\sin\theta_a=\cos\beta/\cos\frac a2$ and $\cos\theta_a=x\sin\theta_a$. Hence the vector part equals $\cos\beta\,(-\varepsilon x(B+C)+B\times C)/(1+p)=-\varepsilon\sin\beta\,X$ by \eqref{eq:X}.
head: environment

label: prop:rotation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rotation}
We have $q_Zq_Yq_X=(-\sin\Phi,\varepsilon\cos\Phi\,B)$. In particular, $R_Z\circ R_Y\circ R_X$ is the rotation about $B$ through the angle $\varepsilon(2\Phi-\pi)$ modulo $2\pi$, and it is the identity if and only if $\cos\Phi=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $\mu_a=-\varepsilon(\pi/2-\theta_a)$, and similarly $\mu_b,\mu_c$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} and the rule $r_V(\lambda)q=q\,r_U(\lambda)$, applied to $h_{CA}$ (which carries $C$ to $A$) and to $h_{BC}$ (which carries $B$ to $C$), we have
\[
q_Zq_Yq_X=h_{AB}r_A(\mu_c)h_{CA}r_C(\mu_b)h_{BC}r_B(\mu_a)
=H\,r_B(\mu_a+\mu_b+\mu_c), \text{ where } H=h_{AB}h_{CA}h_{BC}.
\]
We now compute $H$. Using $\langle C\times A,B\times C\rangle=pq-r$ and $(C\times A)\times(B\times C)=-\delta C$, we find
\[
h_{CA}h_{BC}=\frac{\bigl(\alpha,V\bigr)}{4\cos\frac a2\cos\frac b2},\ \ V=(1+q)\,B\times C+(1+p)\,C\times A-\delta C .
\]
Multiplying by $h_{AB}=(1+r,A\times B)/(2\cos\frac c2)$, and using $\langle A\times B,B\times C\rangle=rp-q$, $\langle A\times B,C\times A\rangle=qr-p$, $\langle A\times B,C\rangle=\delta$ and \eqref{eq:gram}, we see that the real part of $8g\,H$ is
\[
(1+r)\alpha-(1+q)(rp-q)-(1+p)(qr-p)+\delta^2=2\alpha .
\]
Applied from right to left, the three factors of $H$ take $B$ to $C$, then to $A$, and finally back to $B$. Thus $H$ fixes $B$, and its vector part $H_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is a multiple of $B$. The identities
\[
\langle V,B\rangle=\delta,\ \ \langle (A\times B)\times V,B\rangle=\langle A\times B,V\times B\rangle=\delta(1-r)
\]
give $\langle 8g\,H_{\mathrm{vec}},B\rangle=(1+r)\delta+\delta(1-r)=2\delta$. We conclude that $H=(\alpha,\delta B)/(4g)$, which equals $r_B(\Omega/2)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:area}. Since $\mu_a+\mu_b+\mu_c=-\varepsilon(3\pi/2-\Theta)$ and $\Omega/2+\varepsilon\Theta=\varepsilon\Phi$, we deduce that
\[
q_Zq_Yq_X=r_B\Bigl(\frac\Omega2-\varepsilon\frac{3\pi}{2}+\varepsilon\Theta\Bigr)=r_B\Bigl(\varepsilon\bigl(\Phi-\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\bigr)\Bigr)=(-\sin\Phi,\varepsilon\cos\Phi\,B).
\]
The rotation angle is $2\varepsilon(\Phi-3\pi/2)\equiv\varepsilon(2\Phi-\pi)$ modulo $2\pi$, and it vanishes modulo $2\pi$ if and only if $\cos\Phi=0$.
